newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: PRAGUE AND JOHANNESBURG STUCK ON INVESTMENT PACT.
newsitem.headline: PRAGUE AND JOHANNESBURG STUCK ON INVESTMENT PACT.

text.p: Czech and South African trade ministers said on Friday that they were still trying to hammer out an agreement to support and protect bilateral investment which was expected to be signed this week.

"That (agreement) is certainly a complicated affair and thus it must be worked out to a realistically acceptable state for both sides," Czech Industry and Trade Minister Karel Kuhnl told journalist after a meeting his counterpart Alec Erwin.
The Czech side said the new agreement was expected to be signed during Erwin's visit with a South African trade delegation this week.
There was no indication of what was holding up the deal.
Last November the two countries signed an agreement to protect against double taxation in trade involving subjects of both countries.
Total trade was $14.2 million for the first four months of this year, with Prague having a trade deficit with Johannesburg of $4.8 million.
However, in 1996 Prague had a $96 million trade surplus on turnover of $164.2 million mainly due to large shipments of Czech computer technology.

"The capacity of the South African market is significant, and its structure is advantageous for Czech products, which with their relatively good quality and favourable price can compete with foreign suppliers," the Czech ministry said in a statement.
"Currently, the depreciation of the rand is complicating the position of Czech exporters," it added.
The South African rand lost more than 20 percent against the U.S. dollar in 1996 as speculators targeted the currency.
Meanwhile, the Czech crown came under heavy downward pressure last month and has lost about 15 percent of its value since its peak in February against major currencies.

"We've come here as a delegation to strengthen the cooperation between the two economies... Trade is growing slowly, but steadily, and we think that prospects for much better trade are good," Erwin told the news conference.
